title: Cambridge Scientist Marta Shahbazi Killed in Spain Crash En Route to Prize
excerpt: The 41-year-old embryo researcher, a group leader at Cambridge's Laboratory of Molecular Biology, was travelling to collect a scientific excellence award when her train hit another near Urda.
body:
• Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, a group leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, has been confirmed among the 69 people killed in Wednesday's train collision near Urda, south of Madrid.
  • She was travelling to El Rompido, Andalusia, to collect the Spanish Society for Developmental Biology's scientific excellence prize for her work on the earliest stages of human development.
  • Her research examined how human embryos organise themselves and why pregnancies fail; she launched her own laboratory at the LMB in 2020.
  • She is survived by her husband and two young children, aged seven and three; her death was confirmed on Saturday, three days after the crash.

Dr Marta Shahbazi was on her way to collect a prize when the train she was riding hit another near Urda, south of Madrid, on Wednesday, October 28. On Saturday night, after three days in which her family searched hospitals and waited, the authorities confirmed that the 41-year-old Cambridge scientist was among the dead. At least 69 people were killed when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary Iryo train, in one of Europe's worst modern rail disasters and Spain's worst crash since 2013. More than 540 people were aboard the two trains. Our earlier coverage tracked the rescue effort as the toll rose to 69.

A career spent watching life begin

Shahbazi was born in León, Spain, and studied biology and molecular biomedicine at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid before completing her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre. She moved to Cambridge in 2014, joining the laboratory of Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz, where she was a joint first author on work that grew human embryos in the laboratory beyond the stages corresponding to implantation — up to 13 days after fertilisation, far longer than had previously been possible. In 2020 she launched the Shahbazi Lab at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), combining studies of human embryos and stem-cell models to investigate implantation, developmental failure and pregnancy loss. She was also an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute.

"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies."

— MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology

The award she never collected was the 2026 José Luis Gómez-Skarmeta scientific excellence prize from the Spanish Society for Developmental Biology, recognising her outstanding contributions to the study of the early stages of human development; she was due to receive it at the society's conference in El Rompido, Huelva. Just eight days before the crash, she had also been named winner of the 2026 SRUK/CERU Emerging Talent Award. The CiMUS research centre in Santiago de Compostela, where her aunt María José Alonso is a principal investigator, called her a "brilliant young researcher."

"She lived for science and her kids"

Shahbazi lived in Cambridge with her husband, Mirco Petruzzelli, and their children, aged seven and three. The night before the crash, the family had gathered at her parents' home in Madrid. Her brother Carlos told El País, as her fate was still unknown: "My sister Marta is a wonderful, affectionate and happy person, and a tireless worker." The LMB noted that she wrote eloquently about balancing family and career, describing herself as a "mother scientist," and was a much-admired role model for doing so. Her death, the laboratory said, is "a profound shock and a huge loss."

Spain has observed three days of national mourning for the victims of the collision. Investigations into how the two trains came to be on a collision course on the Madrid–Andalusia high-speed line are continuing, and families of the dead are demanding answers.
